_meta.scope: California employment, wage & hour, retaliation, FEHA, and workers' compensation law
_meta.purpose: Controlled reference so a Claude can match a rambled claim to the real statute and compute the statute-of-limitations deadline.
_meta.disclaimer: NOT legal advice. Statute-of-limitations rules have many exceptions (tolling, continuing violations, equitable estoppel, government-claim prerequisites). Every citation and deadline MUST be verified with an attorney before relying on it.

statutes.title: Minimum wage
statutes.covers: Failure to pay at least the legal minimum wage (statewide $16.90/hr effective 2026-01-01; many cities are higher). §1194 lets employees recover unpaid balance plus interest and attorney's fees.
statutes.sol_note: 3 years; reachable back to 4 years when paired with a Bus. & Prof. Code §17200 (UCL) claim.

statutes.title: Overtime
statutes.covers: Unpaid overtime. CA requires 1.5x after 8 hrs/day or 40 hrs/week, and 2x after 12 hrs/day; double time and 7th-consecutive-day rules apply.
statutes.sol_anchor: each pay period overtime went unpaid (rolling)

statutes.title: Meal and rest breaks
statutes.covers: Denied/short/late meal or rest breaks. 30-min unpaid meal per 5 hrs; paid 10-min rest per 4 hrs. Remedy is 1 hour of premium pay per day a meal break was missed and 1 hour per day a rest break was missed.
statutes.sol_anchor: each day a break was missed (rolling)

statutes.title: Final pay / waiting-time penalties
statutes.covers: Final wages not paid on time at end of employment. Discharge = immediate; quit with 72 hrs notice = last day. Penalty is the employee's daily wage for each day late, up to 30 days.
statutes.sol_anchor: end of employment / date final wages were due

statutes.title: Inaccurate wage statements
statutes.covers: Pay stubs missing required info (hours, rates, employer name, etc.). Statutory penalties up to $4,000 plus actual damages.
statutes.sol_anchor: issuance of the defective wage statement
statutes.sol_note: 1 year for §226 penalties; underlying wage damages can reach 3 years.

statutes.title: Business expense reimbursement
statutes.covers: Failure to reimburse necessary business expenses (mileage, phone, tools, remote-work costs). Employer cannot push operating costs onto employees.

statutes.title: Whistleblower retaliation
statutes.covers: Retaliation for disclosing, or refusing to participate in, what the employee reasonably believes is a legal violation — to a government agency, to a supervisor, or internally. 90-day rebuttable presumption of retaliation if adverse action follows protected activity within 90 days.
statutes.sol_anchor: date of the retaliatory act (e.g., termination)

statutes.title: Retaliation for wage complaints / protected conduct
statutes.covers: Retaliation for complaining about unpaid wages, filing a Labor Commissioner claim, or other protected conduct under the Labor Code.
statutes.sol_note: Generally 3 years; a DLSE administrative claim has a shorter window (often cited as ~6 months) — verify the path.

statutes.title: Health & safety complaint retaliation / right to refuse unsafe work
statutes.covers: Retaliation for complaining about unsafe working conditions (Cal/OSHA), and the right to refuse work that would violate a safety standard and create a real and apparent hazard.
statutes.sol_note: Civil suit generally 3 years; a Labor Commissioner complaint has a shorter window — verify.

statutes.title: Workers' compensation retaliation
statutes.covers: Discrimination or retaliation because an employee filed (or intends to file) a workers' comp claim, or testified in another's claim. Remedies: up to $10,000 added comp, reinstatement, lost wages/benefits; it is also a misdemeanor.
statutes.sol_note: 1 YEAR to file a petition with the WCAB — short and hard. Missing it almost always means dismissal.
statutes.procedural_note: Filed as a petition with the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board (WCAB), not a regular civil court.

statutes.title: Workers' compensation injury claim
statutes.covers: Benefits for a work-related injury or illness (medical care, temporary/permanent disability, etc.). The exclusive remedy against the employer for most on-the-job injuries.
statutes.sol_anchor: date of injury (or last date of a cumulative/continuous trauma)
statutes.sol_note: Generally 1 year from the date of injury to file the claim; extended for cumulative trauma and where the employer failed to provide a claim form. Filed with the WCAB.
statutes.procedural_note: Workers' Compensation Appeals Board (WCAB). Separate from a civil lawsuit.

statutes.title: FEHA — employment discrimination
statutes.covers: Discrimination in hiring, firing, pay, or terms because of a protected characteristic (race, sex, age 40+, disability, religion, national origin, sexual orientation, gender identity, medical condition, etc.).
statutes.sol_note: Must FIRST file a complaint with the Civil Rights Department (CRD) within 3 years of the act, THEN sue within 1 year of the right-to-sue notice.
statutes.procedural_note: Administrative exhaustion required: CRD complaint + right-to-sue letter before a civil suit.

statutes.title: FEHA — harassment / hostile work environment
statutes.covers: Harassment based on a protected characteristic, including a hostile work environment and sexual harassment. Employers are liable for supervisor harassment; individual harassers can be personally liable.
statutes.sol_note: CRD complaint within 3 years of the last incident, then 1 year from right-to-sue to file suit.

statutes.title: FEHA — retaliation
statutes.covers: Retaliation for opposing FEHA-prohibited conduct, or for filing/testifying/assisting in a FEHA proceeding. Protection applies if the employee reasonably and in good faith believed the conduct was unlawful.
statutes.sol_note: CRD complaint within 3 years, then 1 year from right-to-sue to sue.

statutes.title: FEHA — failure to accommodate / interactive process
statutes.covers: Failure to provide reasonable accommodation for a disability (m), and failure to engage in a timely, good-faith interactive process to find one (n).
statutes.sol_anchor: date accommodation was denied / process failed
statutes.sol_note: CRD complaint within 3 years, then 1 year from right-to-sue to sue.
statutes.procedural_note: Administrative exhaustion via CRD required. Often pairs with a workers'-comp injury that left medical restrictions.

statutes.title: California Family Rights Act leave
statutes.covers: Interference with or retaliation for taking protected family/medical leave (own serious health condition, family care, baby bonding) at employers with 5+ employees.
statutes.sol_note: CRD complaint within 3 years, then 1 year from right-to-sue to sue.

statutes.title: Wrongful termination in violation of public policy
statutes.covers: Firing an employee for a reason that violates a fundamental public policy (e.g., for filing a workers' comp claim, refusing to do something illegal, reporting unsafe conditions, taking protected leave). A standalone tort.
statutes.sol_note: 2 years (personal-injury limitations period, CCP §335.1). No CRD exhaustion required for the public-policy tort itself.

statutes.title: Private Attorneys General Act
statutes.covers: Lets an aggrieved employee sue for civil penalties for Labor Code violations on behalf of the state and other employees. Often stacked on wage-and-hour claims.
statutes.sol_anchor: date of the underlying Labor Code violation
statutes.sol_note: 1 year, but you must first send written notice to the LWDA and the employer and satisfy a waiting period before filing. The notice deadline is strict.
statutes.procedural_note: Mandatory LWDA online notice + exhaustion before suit.
